concepts.title: Werner's Theory and Valences
concepts.definition: Werner's theory describes coordination complexes by assigning two types of valences to the metal: ionizable primary valences and non-ionizable secondary valences.
concepts.key_idea: Primary valences correspond to the oxidation state, while secondary valences correspond to the coordination number.
question_patterns: determine the secondary valence of the metal from precipitation data
calculate the secondary valence of the central metal in the compound

solution_steps.action: Calculate the number of coordinated anions inside the coordination sphere
solution_steps.explain: Subtract the number of precipitated anions from the total number of anions in the formula.

solution_steps.action: Sum the coordinated anions and neutral ligands to find the secondary valence
solution_steps.explain: The secondary valence is the total number of ligands directly coordinated to the metal.

solution_steps.action: Verify the primary valence from the precipitated anions
solution_steps.explain: The number of ionisable (primary) valences equals the count of anions precipitated by AgNO3, confirming the oxidation state of the metal.

concepts.title: Coordination Number of Central Metal
concepts.definition: How many ligand donor atoms are bonded straight to the central metal ion.
concepts.key_idea: The coordination number varies with both the number of ligands and their individual denticities.
question_patterns: find the coordination number of the metal in the complex
calculate the coordination number of the central atom

solution_steps.action: Compute the total coordination number from the ligands
solution_steps.explain: Multiply each ligand count by its respective denticity and sum the products.

solution_steps.action: Identify the denticity of each ligand type
solution_steps.explain: Monodentate ligands (e.g. Cl-, NH3) donate one donor atom each, while bidentate (e.g. en, ox) donate two and hexadentate (e.g. EDTA) donate six.

solution_steps.action: Verify the coordination number against the metal geometry
solution_steps.explain: Common coordination numbers are 4 (tetrahedral or square planar) and 6 (octahedral); the computed value should match one of these expected geometries.

concepts.title: Oxidation State of Central Metal
concepts.definition: The charge that the central metal atom would carry if all ligands were indeed removed together with the electron pairs shared with them.
concepts.key_idea: The charges on the metal ion and all ligands add up to the overall charge of the coordination entity.
question_patterns: calculate the oxidation number of the central metal

solution_steps.action: Calculate the total charge contributed by the ligands
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the count of each ligand by its charge and sum them up.

solution_steps.action: Determine the oxidation state of the metal
solution_steps.explain: Subtract the total ligand charge from the overall charge of the complex.

solution_steps.action: Verify the oxidation state is chemically reasonable
solution_steps.explain: Check that the calculated oxidation state is a common or known stable state for the given metal (e.g. Fe2+/Fe3+, Co3+, Pt2+), ensuring the charge balance of the entire complex is correct.

concepts.title: IUPAC Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds
concepts.definition: Systematic rules established by IUPAC for naming coordination complexes, where ligands are named alphabetically as prefixes followed by the central metal and its oxidation state.
concepts.key_idea: The cation is indeed named first, ligands are listed alphabetically, and the metal's oxidation state is written in Roman numerals.

solution_steps.action: Determine the oxidation state of the central metal

solution_steps.action: List and name the ligands alphabetically
solution_steps.explain: Use prefixes like di-, tri-, tetra- or bis-, tris- to indicate ligand quantities, and name them in alphabetical order.

solution_steps.action: Assemble the full name
solution_steps.explain: Combine the ligand names with the metal name (ending in -ate if the complex is anionic) and the oxidation state in parentheses.

concepts.title: Isomerism in Coordination Compounds
concepts.definition: The existence of coordination compounds with identical molecular formulas but different structural arrangements or spatial orientations of their atoms.
concepts.key_idea: Isomers are classified into structural isomers (linkage, coordination, ionisation, solvate) and stereoisomers (geometrical, optical).

solution_steps.action: Analyze the chemical formula and coordination sphere
solution_steps.explain: Check for the presence of ambidentate ligands, exchangeable counter-ions, or different metal centers.

solution_steps.action: Determine the coordination geometry
solution_steps.explain: Identify if the complex is square planar or octahedral to evaluate stereochemical possibilities.

solution_steps.action: Check for symmetry and chirality
solution_steps.explain: If the complex lacks a plane of symmetry (typically cis-octahedral with didentate ligands), it exhibits optical isomerism.

concepts.title: Valence Bond Theory and Hybridisation
concepts.definition: A bonding theory stating that the metal ion provides empty hybrid orbitals of definite geometry to accept electron pairs donated by ligands.
concepts.key_idea: The coordination number determines the hybridisation scheme (sp3, dsp2, d2sp3, or sp3d2) and the resulting spatial geometry.

solution_steps.action: Find the oxidation state and electronic configuration of the metal ion
solution_steps.explain: Determine the number of d-electrons remaining on the central metal ion.

solution_steps.action: Assess the field strength of the ligands
solution_steps.explain: Strong-field ligands (like CN-, CO) cause pairing of d-electrons, while weak-field ligands (like Cl-, F-) do not.

solution_steps.action: Identify the hybridisation type
solution_steps.explain: Select vacant (n-1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals to accommodate the ligand electron pairs.

solution_steps.action: Deduce the geometry and magnetic nature
solution_steps.explain: Assign geometry (tetrahedral, square planar, octahedral) and determine if the complex is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.

concepts.title: Spin-Only Magnetic Moment
concepts.definition: The magnetic moment of a coordination complex calculated from the number of unpaired d-electrons on the central metal ion.
concepts.key_idea: The magnetic moment grows with the number of unpaired both electrons and is measured in Bohr Magnetons (BM).
question_patterns: calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of
find the magnetic moment of the complex with unpaired electrons
predict the magnetic moment in Bohr Magnetons for
find the required value in a spin-only magnetic moment problem
solve a numerical on spin-only magnetic moment

solution_steps.action: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment
solution_steps.explain: Apply the formula mu = sqrt(n * (n + 2)) where n is the number of unpaired electrons.

solution_steps.action: Determine the number of unpaired electrons from the d-electron count
solution_steps.explain: Find the d^n configuration of the metal ion and distribute electrons according to the ligand field strength (high-spin or low-spin) to obtain n, the count of unpaired electrons.

solution_steps.action: Express the result in Bohr Magnetons and interpret
solution_steps.explain: Report mu in BM units; a value of zero indicates a diamagnetic complex, while a non-zero value indicates paramagnetism that increases with the number of unpaired electrons.

concepts.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Octahedral Complexes
concepts.definition: The split of the five degenerate d-orbitals into a lower-energy t2g set and a higher-energy eg set, caused by electrostatic repulsion in an octahedral ligand field.
concepts.key_idea: The configuration of d4 to d7 ions hangs on the relative sizes of the crystal-field splitting energy (delta_o) and the pairing energy (P).
question_patterns: explain the crystal field splitting in an octahedral complex
write the electronic configuration of d4 ion in octahedral field when delta_o is greater than P
determine the d-orbital configuration of the metal in octahedral field
explain crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes in your own words
describe crystal field splitting in octahedral complexes with an example

solution_steps.action: Determine the number of d-electrons on the metal ion
solution_steps.explain: Find the oxidation state and write the corresponding d^n configuration.

solution_steps.action: Compare the splitting energy (delta_o) with the pairing energy (P)
solution_steps.explain: If delta_o > P, it is a strong-field/low-spin complex. If delta_o < P, it is a weak-field/high-spin complex.

solution_steps.action: Distribute electrons into t2g and eg orbitals
solution_steps.explain: Fill the lower t2g orbitals first, pairing electrons if in a strong field, or placing them in eg if in a weak field.

concepts.title: Crystal Field Splitting in Tetrahedral Complexes
concepts.definition: The splitting of d-orbitals in a tetrahedral ligand field where the e set is lower in energy and the t2 set is higher in energy, with a smaller splitting magnitude than in octahedral fields.
concepts.key_idea: Because the tetrahedral splitting energy is small, electrons do not pair up easily, making low-spin tetrahedral complexes extremely rare.
question_patterns: calculate the tetrahedral crystal field splitting energy from octahedral splitting
what is the relation between tetrahedral and octahedral splitting energy
find the value of delta_t given delta_o
work out the value using crystal field splitting in tetrahedral complexes
calculate crystal field splitting in tetrahedral complexes for the given values

solution_steps.action: Calculate the tetrahedral splitting energy
solution_steps.explain: Multiply the octahedral splitting energy by 4/9 to obtain the tetrahedral splitting energy.

solution_steps.action: Identify the orbital energy ordering in a tetrahedral field
solution_steps.explain: In a tetrahedral field the e set is lower in energy and the t2 set is higher, which is the reverse of the octahedral splitting pattern.

solution_steps.action: Explain why low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rare
solution_steps.explain: Because delta_t is only 4/9 of delta_o and is smaller than the pairing energy P, electrons prefer to occupy higher-energy orbitals rather than pair up, so tetrahedral complexes are almost always high-spin.

concepts.title: Synergic Bonding in Metal Carbonyls
concepts.definition: A self-strengthening bonding mechanism in metal carbonyls involving sigma-donation from ligand to both metal and simultaneous pi-backdonation from metal to ligand.
concepts.key_idea: The synergic effect strengthens both the metal-carbon both bond and weakens the carbon-oxygen bond.
question_patterns: explain the nature of bonding in metal carbonyls
what is synergic effect in coordination compounds
describe the synergic bonding in
describe synergic bonding in metal carbonyls with an example
what do you understand by synergic bonding in metal carbonyls

solution_steps.action: Describe the metal-carbon sigma bond
solution_steps.explain: The carbonyl carbon donates its lone pair of electrons into a vacant metal d-orbital.

solution_steps.action: Describe the metal-carbon pi bond
solution_steps.explain: Filled metal d-orbitals donate electron density back into the vacant antibonding pi* orbitals of CO.

solution_steps.action: Explain the synergic reinforcement
solution_steps.explain: The sigma donation increases electron density on the metal, which in turn enhances its ability to back-donate via pi-bonding.
